Non-Uniqueness in Sketching a Function Given the Graph of Its Derivative
?

Let's draw our possible function once more. The graph of its derivative is also shown.

In reality, there are infinitely many possible graphs of that can be drawn if we are given only the graph of We can always shift the graph up and down as we please, because the slopes of the tangent lines do not change. For the problem above, any of the following graphs would be valid:

In this topic, we will focus on sketching a possible graph of given the graph of But bear in mind that whatever we sketch, we can get an equally valid answer by shifting or curve up or down by an arbitrary amount.

The only exception is if we're given a point on the curve If we're given a point, this has the effect of fixing our answer to a particular curve. We'll see an example of this next.

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that critical points of y=f(x) occur when f′(x)=0 or f′(x) does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points:

x=−1 and x=0.

Also, we have the following:

  • If f′(x)>0 then f(x) is increasing.

  • If f′(x)<0 then f(x) is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

x (−∞,−1) −1 (−1,0) 0 (0,∞)
f′ − 0 − 0 +
f ↘ not extr. ↘ min ↗

Let's now sketch the graph of y=f(x):

  • First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines x=−1, and x=0.

    • Since we are told that f(0)=0, we can draw that point on the graph.

    • Since f(x) is decreasing ↘ on (−1,0), the point at x=0 must be lower than the point at x=−1.

    So, we draw it as follows:

  • Next, we consider the behavior of y=f(x) in the neighborhood of the critical points:

    • Since f(x) is decreasing ↘ on (−∞,−1) and on (−1,0), the graph of y=f(x) goes up to the left and down to the right of x=−1.

    • Since f(x) is decreasing ↘ on (−1,0) and increasing ↗ on (0,∞), the graph of y=f(x) goes up to the left and to the right of x=0.

  • Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of y=f(x):
